item.title: Thermodynamic Proof of Quantumness without Structure
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Any classical machine solving the structureless Yamakawa–Zhandry search problem with constant success probability must generate entropy S[ρ]≥Θ(λ2λc), requiring exponential Landauer heat dissipation and energy consumption W≥kBTS[ρ], whereas the quantum solver needs only polynomial energy.

Grade 0.431 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum algorithms with provable speedup, query and gate complexity bounds” · Florian Meier, Hayata Yamasaki

Figure

Classical energy-consumption lower bound kBTS at T=300 K versus security parameter λ, compared against macroscopic benchmarks like CERN annual energy consumption.

Asks

Does the exponential quantum advantage for unstructured search persist for macroscopic physical resources like energy consumption?

Before

Exponential quantum energy advantage was proven only for Simon's problem with a highly structured oracle (Meier & Yamasaki 2024), leaving unstructured search open.

But

Asymptotic security parameter λ, random oracle model, constant success probability Δ>0, cyclic computation reset to standard initial state.

Tools

Yamakawa–Zhandry search problem · Landauer's principle · random oracle model · stopping-time entropy minimization

Abstract

Demonstrating that a machine performs genuinely quantum operations is a central challenge in quantum information processing. Existing proofs of quantumness typically rely on computational tasks that are infeasible for classical machines under assumptions such as computational hardness, or explicit bounds on classical runtime, memory, or oracle queries. Here we introduce an alternative paradigm: a thermodynamic proof of quantumness based on energy consumption. Using the search problem of Yamakawa and Zhandry with a structureless uniformly random oracle, we show that any classical machine solving the task with constant success probability must generate entropy that grows exponentially with the security parameter. By Landauer's principle, this implies an exponential lower bound on heat dissipation and hence on the energy consumption of any cyclic classical implementation. In contrast, the corresponding quantum prover solves the task with polynomial query and gate complexity, giving polynomial energy consumption under standard assumptions for quantum implementations. Thus, in the random-oracle setting, sufficiently low energy consumption in a successful implementation certifies quantumness through a macroscopic thermodynamic observation of energy consumption.

item.title: When Quantum Meets AI: Quantum Methods for Machine Learning and Machine Learning Methods for Quantum Systems
item.description:
Worth a look review — Mamba-based neural decoder matches Transformer accuracy on surface codes while dropping inference-cost scaling from quartic to quadratic in code distance. Multi-shift stochastic reconfiguration reduces validation residuals and update variance in neural quantum states.

Grade 0.417 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum singular value transformation and beyond: exponential improvements for…” · Tak Hur

Asks

How do learned representations, statistical regularization, and hardware constraints optimize quantum machine learning and classical neural methods for quantum error correction and simulation?

Before

Transformer neural decoders scaled quartically with surface code distance; fixed-shift stochastic reconfiguration suffered from sample-noise trade-offs.

But

NMR demonstrations limited to small-scale DQC1; multi-shift SR adds computational cost; Mamba decoder evaluated under specific decoder-induced noise models.

Tools

Neural Quantum Embedding · DQC1 on NMR processor · Mamba state-space decoder · multi-shift stochastic reconfiguration

Abstract

This thesis studies the intersection of quantum computing and artificial intelligence in two directions: quantum methods for machine learning and machine learning methods for quantum systems. For quantum machine learning, Neural Quantum Embedding learns data representations that increase the trace distance between embedded class ensembles, lowering an embedding-dependent bound on empirical risk and improving classification on noisy quantum hardware. A training objective based on the Hilbert-Schmidt inner product extends this approach to deterministic quantum computation with one qubit (DQC1) and is demonstrated on an NMR quantum processor. A margin-based generalization analysis then connects quantum neural network performance to quantum state discrimination. In the studied benchmarks, margin distributions predict generalization more reliably than parameter-count metrics. For quantum systems, a Mamba-based neural decoder for surface codes matches a reproduced Transformer baseline in memory experiments while reducing inference-cost scaling from quartic to quadratic in code distance. Under an explicit decoder-induced-noise model, it achieves lower logical error rates and a higher effective threshold. For neural quantum states, stochastic reconfiguration is interpreted as tangent-space ridge regression, with its diagonal shift controlling the bias-variance trade-off under finite Monte Carlo sampling. Multi-shift stochastic reconfiguration reduces checkpoint-local validation residuals and update variance relative to fixed-shift SR, at additional computational cost. Together, these contributions show how learned representations, statistical control, and hardware constraints shape the exchange between quantum computing and machine learning.

item.title: Tensor Network Simulation of Dynamic Circuits
item.description:
Long shot new method — DMRG-based tensor network simulation natively evaluates dynamic circuits via single-path stochastic sampling and multi-path branch ensemble tracking on MPS and TTN structures, achieving scalable branch propagation with bounded peak memory on 27-qubit random circuits.

Grade 0.393 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Innocenzo Fulginiti, Alessandro Poggiali, Christian Mendl

Figure

Runtime (left) and peak memory usage (right) versus qubit count for dynamic GHZ state preparation comparing unpruned multi-path simulation against single-path sampling with 16, 64, and 256 runs.

Asks

How can tensor-network DMRG algorithms be extended to classically simulate dynamic quantum circuits with mid-circuit measurements and classical feedforward without exponential path overhead?

But

Evaluated up to 27 qubits and depth 8; fixed bond dimensions χ∈{8,16,32}; multi-path branch count capped at M=8.

Tools

DMRG quantum circuit simulation · Matrix Product States (MPS) · Tree Tensor Networks (TTN) · Single-path stochastic sampling · Multi-path branch pruning

Abstract

Dynamic circuits, which incorporate mid-circuit measurements and classically controlled operations, extend the expressive power of quantum programs and are central to applications such as quantum error correction, state preparation, and distributed quantum algorithms. However, their classical simulation is challenging due to the exponential growth of execution branches induced by mid-circuit measurements. In this work, we develop a tensor network approach for simulating dynamic circuits by extending a DMRG-based method for quantum circuit simulation to support dynamic circuit operations. To address the exponential proliferation of execution branches, we introduce and compare two strategies: a single-path stochastic approach that samples individual measurement outcomes, and a multi-path approach that maintains an ensemble of branches. We benchmark these methods on standard dynamic circuits, including the teleportation protocol and GHZ state preparation, as well as on random dynamic circuits. Our analysis explores the trade-offs between simulation accuracy and computational efficiency. These results provide a practical and scalable framework for the classical simulation of dynamic circuits.
